name: Dot (New Computer)
one_line: A personalized AI companion app that built a long-term memory of your life and acted as a confidant/'inner voice'.
audience: Consumers, heavily skewed to young adults using it as an emotional confidant and journaling companion.
stated_cause: Co-founders Sam Whitmore and Jason Yuan said their 'long-term visions for the product had diverged' and chose to wind down New Computer entirely rather than compromise either direction; coverage tied the timing to safety scrutiny of companion apps and the economics of subsidizing inference against modest subscription revenue.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Cheap 2026 inference removes the cost-subsidy pressure, but the actual stated cause was founder/vision divergence plus a companion-safety regime that in 2026 is tighter, not looser - no capability change dissolves that.

name: Humane AI Pin
one_line: A $699 wearable screenless AI assistant with a laser projector meant to replace the phone for queries, messaging and photos.
audience: Early-adopter consumers who wanted to be 'off' their smartphone; tech-forward professionals.
stated_cause: HP bought Humane's IP, patents and most staff for $116M; Humane discontinued the Pin immediately and cut servers on 2025-02-28. The device had targeted 100,000 units and sold roughly 10,000 - reviews were brutal and the hardware ran hot, slow and short on battery.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly. 2026 on-device and low-latency hosted models fix the latency and cost problems that made the Pin unusable, but the demand problem - nobody needed a second, worse device beside a phone they already carry - is untouched by any model capability.

name: Jibo
one_line: The 'world's first social robot' - a swiveling tabletop companion that recognized family members and chatted proactively.
audience: Families with kids and older adults; $899 early-adopter households from a record-setting Indiegogo campaign.
stated_cause: The company burned through roughly $73M, laid off most staff, sold its IP and shut off the cloud servers that ran Jibo's brain; it could not compete on price or capability with Alexa and Google Home, shipped years late, and a pivot to enterprise failed.
dissolved_by_2026: No. 2026 models would make Jibo genuinely conversational, which was its weakest point, but it still dies to a $40 smart speaker doing 80% of the job - the price/utility gap against platform incumbents is not a model capability problem.

name: Moxie (Embodied Inc.)
one_line: An $799 cloud-connected social robot that ran daily emotional-learning and conversation sessions with children.
audience: Parents of children aged 5-10, with a strong following among families of neurodivergent kids.
stated_cause: Embodied told customers a critical funding round collapsed: a lead investor 'at the last minute ... withdrew, leaving us with no viable options.' No replacement was found, no refunds were offered, and the cloud servers that held the robot's intelligence were switched off on 2025-01-30, bricking every unit.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly. Cheap 2026 inference plus on-device small models would let a Moxie-class robot run without a per-unit cloud bill, dissolving the cost side - but the capital intensity of consumer hardware and an investor walking away is a financing failure no model capability removes.

name: Kuri (Mayfield Robotics)
one_line: A $799 home companion robot that roamed the house, recognized faces, played media and captured family moments.
audience: Affluent US families with children; pre-order early adopters.
stated_cause: Bosch-backed Mayfield cancelled Kuri and ceased operations: after talking to 'many dozens of companies' it was 'unable to reach an agreement' on financing, and Bosch found 'there was not a business fit within Bosch to support and scale our business.'
dissolved_by_2026: No. Kuri was killed before it ever had a cloud bill - a corporate parent decided home robots had no viable business. 2026 capability makes the robot smarter but does not create the demand or margin that Bosch could not find.

name: Anki Vector / Cozmo
one_line: Palm-sized autonomous companion robots with personality, voice interaction and an Alexa integration.
audience: Consumers and families buying a $250 desk companion / toy robot; 1.5M units sold across product lines.
stated_cause: CEO Boris Sofman told staff a new financing round 'failed to materialize at the last minute,' as did acquisition interest from Microsoft, Amazon and Comcast. Anki had raised ~$200M; it laid off all ~200 employees. Hardware cost with no recurring software revenue could not bridge to the long-term roadmap.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly. The specific gap - hardware margin with no recurring revenue - is now plausibly closed by a subscription-worthy 2026 assistant running on the device, but the last-minute financing collapse and the absence of a repeat-purchase reason remain untouched.

name: Mycroft AI
one_line: An open-source, privacy-respecting voice assistant and the Mark II smart speaker, positioned as an Alexa/Google Home alternative.
audience: Privacy-conscious consumers, Linux/maker hobbyists, Kickstarter backers.
stated_cause: The CEO told backers the company was out of money and could not fulfil remaining Mark II Kickstarter rewards; he named 'ongoing litigation against the non-practicing patent entity' (a patent troll) as the single most expensive line item that drained the company.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Local 2026 models make an open-source assistant vastly more capable and cheaper to run, but Mycroft died of hardware cash burn and legal defense costs. Patent litigation and Kickstarter hardware economics are unaffected by model capability.

name: Facebook M
one_line: A human-plus-AI personal assistant inside Messenger that would book, buy, plan and research anything you asked.
audience: A capped beta of a few thousand Bay Area Messenger users; intended eventually for all Messenger users.
stated_cause: Facebook shut the standalone assistant down, keeping only the lightweight 'M suggestions' in Messenger. M never scaled past a small test group because every hard request fell through to human trainers; Facebook framed it as a research project whose learnings would move into automated suggestions.
dissolved_by_2026: Yes, mostly. The blocking cause was that humans had to backstop nearly every request - 2026 tool-using agents genuinely close that gap for booking, ordering and research. What it does not dissolve: users treating an open-ended 'ask me anything' box as a novelty rather than a habit.

name: x.ai (Amy / Andrew Ingram)
one_line: An AI meeting scheduler you CC'd on an email thread; 'Amy' negotiated times, sent follow-ups and handled cancellations.
audience: Sales reps, recruiters, executives and consultants who scheduled many external meetings by email.
stated_cause: Bizzabo acquired x.ai in June 2021 and shut the standalone product down on 2021-10-31, saying it would 'prioritize building x.ai's powerful scheduling and recommendations directly into Bizzabo's event management platform.' The underlying business had been squeezed between free scheduling links (Calendly) and the cost of the human-in-the-loop review layer.
dissolved_by_2026: No. 2026 LLMs make email-thread scheduling trivially reliable and remove the human reviewers entirely - but the product was already outcompeted by a free scheduling link that required no AI at all. Better AI does not beat 'just send a Calendly'.

name: Clara Labs (Clara)
one_line: An email-based AI scheduling assistant with human review, later repositioned for recruiting coordination.
audience: Recruiters, hiring managers and busy executives; sold per-seat at premium prices.
stated_cause: Acquired by recruiting-software firm TopFunnel two years after a $7M round and folded in; Clara ceased operating as an independent consumer/prosumer product. The model - AI with humans handling edge cases - was expensive to run, locked to a single narrow use case, and could not expand beyond scheduling.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly. The human-in-the-loop cost layer genuinely dissolves with 2026 agents. The narrowness problem does not: scheduling alone was never a large enough wedge to build a company on, and that is a market-size fact, not a capability gap.

name: GoButler
one_line: A free SMS concierge - text one number and human assistants would book, buy or arrange anything for you.
audience: Urban consumers in the US and Germany; venture-funded free-to-use growth.
stated_cause: GoButler killed the open-ended human assistant and pivoted to a narrow, 'fully-automated service' for flight search, saying automation via NLP was 'an important step in creating a company with scalability and longevity' and that 'the original digital assistant service will no longer be available.' It had already paused Germany to focus on the US.
dissolved_by_2026: Yes, on the cost axis only. 2026 agents can do the open-ended fulfillment that humans were doing at negative margin. But GoButler was free with no revenue model - cheap inference makes the losses smaller, not the business real.

name: Fin (Fin Exploration Company)
one_line: A voice-and-text personal assistant blending trained human operators with software, billed hourly for open-ended life admin.
audience: High-income professionals and founders outsourcing scheduling, research, travel and errands.
stated_cause: Fin retired the consumer assistant and pivoted to Fin Analytics, workplace productivity analytics. Despite a highly efficient ops team, the service was still 'more expensive than most customers wanted' - the human labour floor under each request never dropped below what consumers would pay.
dissolved_by_2026: Yes, for the stated cause. The binding constraint was the human cost per request, which 2026 tool-using agents remove almost entirely. What is not dissolved: the founders also found demand was concentrated in a thin band of very rich users.

name: Zirtual
one_line: A subscription marketplace pairing consumers and small businesses with a dedicated US-based virtual assistant.
audience: Solopreneurs, executives and busy professionals paying $400-$1,500/month for delegated life and work admin.
stated_cause: Zirtual shut down overnight and laid off 400+ staff by email. Founder Maren Kate Donovan cited the burn: switching assistants from contractors to full-time employees in January 2015 pushed burn to roughly $400K/month, and a $3M round collapsed days before closing. (Assets were later bought by Startups.co and relaunched.)
dissolved_by_2026: Yes, for the labour cost. The whole company was a human-wage arbitrage that never worked; 2026 agents do most of that task list at near-zero marginal cost. What survives as a hard problem: the tasks customers most valued were the judgment-heavy ones, and trust in delegation, not capability, gated adoption.

name: Pi (Inflection AI)
one_line: A warm, emotionally attentive personal AI chatbot positioned as a supportive companion rather than a productivity tool.
audience: General consumers seeking a kind, conversational AI for reflection, advice and company.
stated_cause: After Microsoft hired Mustafa Suleyman and nearly all of Inflection's 70-person team in March 2024, the remaining company capped Pi and pivoted to a B2B, API-first model. The public reasoning: giants with ~$100B in cash could give away consumer AI free, an arms race no consumer-AI startup could fund.
dissolved_by_2026: No - and it is the sharpest counterexample. Inference got cheap for Inflection and for OpenAI, Google and Meta simultaneously. Cheap capability is not a moat; free distribution from an incumbent is, and 2026 made that worse.

name: Donna (Incredible Labs)
one_line: A proactive mobile assistant that read your calendar and told you when to leave, who you were meeting and how to reach them.
audience: iPhone-owning professionals with meeting-heavy calendars.
stated_cause: Yahoo acqui-hired Incredible Labs for mobile talent and pulled Donna from the App Store about a month later; five of seven staff joined Yahoo Mail. Donna emailed users that she was 'retiring as an assistant.' The product was never given a chance to find a business - it was bought for the team.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Donna's features (leave-now alerts, meeting context) are commodity 2026 capability and shipped inside every calendar app - which is exactly the problem. The cause of death was being a small standalone app in a category incumbents absorb, and that pattern is stronger in 2026.

name: Essential Products / Project Gem
one_line: Andy Rubin's 'AI-first' ultra-narrow phone built around a predictive assistant meant to handle tasks instead of apps.
audience: Consumers frustrated by app-juggling smartphones; Essential Phone (PH-1) owners.
stated_cause: Essential ceased operations, saying that despite best efforts it had 'no clear path to deliver' Project Gem to customers. The PH-1 got its last security update and all support ended. Funding and reputational fallout around Rubin also foreclosed further raises.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly. The assistant-instead-of-apps interface Gem promised is technically achievable with 2026 agent models. The distribution reality is not: shipping a new phone OS against iOS and Android is a platform problem, not a model problem.

name: Monaru
one_line: A human-plus-software relationship concierge that planned dates, gifts and check-ins for your closest 10-15 people.
audience: Millennials in relationships who wanted to be more thoughtful to partners, family and close friends.
stated_cause: Co-founder Pat Finegan's public account frames the wind-down around founder burnout after repeated pivots ('it felt like slowly sinking'), a small $150K seed, and an inability to get the product past pivot stage; Crunchbase lists the company as dead.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Monaru never found a repeatable reason for users to keep paying for thoughtfulness-as-a-service. 2026 agents can draft the message and buy the gift, but the failure was that people who want to be thoughtful don't want it outsourced - a preference, not a capability.

name: UpHabit
one_line: A personal CRM that reminded you to reach out to people in your network before the relationship went cold.
audience: Networkers, salespeople and relationship-minded professionals; later repositioned toward 'relationship selling' and Salesforce.
stated_cause: The shutdown notice on uphabit.com: 'while we succeeded on a product level, it wasn't a commercial success so we've made the difficult decision to close down the web and mobile apps.' Web and mobile apps closed 2026-04-09.
dissolved_by_2026: No, and this is the cleanest case. UpHabit shut down in 2026, with 2026 capability fully available. The product worked; people would not pay for it. Nothing about model quality changes willingness-to-pay for nagging.

name: Garden: Stay in Touch
one_line: A solo-developer iOS app that grouped contacts into 'keep in touch' tiers and nudged you when someone was overdue.
audience: Individuals wanting to maintain friendships and family ties deliberately.
stated_cause: No formal shutdown notice - the app was simply abandoned, with the last update on 2020-06-04 and no maintenance since. A textbook single-maintainer personal-CRM death: no revenue to justify continued work.
dissolved_by_2026: No. A solo dev can ship a far better version in 2026 in a weekend, which makes abandonment more likely, not less - supply of these apps was never the constraint, sustained user demand was.

name: Humin
one_line: A contacts app that indexed people by context - 'met last week in SF', 'works at X' - instead of alphabetically, plus Knock Knock for swapping details.
audience: Heavy networkers, conference-goers and professionals in relationship-driven jobs; raised ~$15M.
stated_cause: Tinder acqui-hired Humin; Humin and Knock Knock were wound down as standalone services with the founders joining Tinder as VPs. The app had limited traction in a crowded contact-management space and was struggling to raise further capital.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Humin's core hard problem - getting a rich, current picture of your relationships - is helped by 2026 models reading your comms with permission. But it died because a contacts app cannot get enough users to matter next to the OS address book, which is a distribution fact.

name: Refresh.io
one_line: A 'digital briefing book' that assembled a dossier on whoever you were about to meet, from calendar plus social data.
audience: Salespeople, recruiters, executives and anyone with back-to-back external meetings; raised $10M.
stated_cause: LinkedIn acquired Refresh for its predictive-insights team, stopped new signups and shut the app down on 2015-04-15; 12 of 15 staff moved to LinkedIn. The technology became a feature of LinkedIn's anticipatory computing efforts rather than a standalone product.
dissolved_by_2026: No. 2026 models write a better pre-meeting brief than Refresh ever did - and every calendar and CRM ships one for free. The cause of death was that this is a feature of a platform that owns the professional graph, and LinkedIn still owns it.

name: Timeful
one_line: A behavioural-science smart calendar that auto-scheduled your intentions, habits and to-dos into real time slots.
audience: iOS users trying to actually do the things on their list; built with Dan Ariely as a co-founder.
stated_cause: Google acquired Timeful in May 2015 to fold its scheduling intelligence into Google Apps; the standalone app was discontinued and the team moved to internal Google projects. The suggestion engine later surfaced as Google Calendar Goals.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Auto-scheduling your intentions is now a table-stakes feature in Google and Microsoft calendars. Timeful's problem was that the best version of its product belongs to whoever owns the calendar, and 2026 does not change calendar ownership.

name: Sunrise Calendar
one_line: A beloved cross-platform calendar with deep third-party connectors and a natural-language 'Meet' assistant.
audience: Mobile-first professionals on iOS/Android/Mac; several million users at acquisition.
stated_cause: Microsoft bought Sunrise for ~$100M in 2015 and announced the app would be discontinued and its functionality merged into Outlook Mobile; the app stopped working on 2016-09-13 once the Outlook calendar redesign shipped.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Sunrise was not capability-limited at all - it was absorbed. Standalone calendar clients keep dying into the mail/calendar suite that owns the account, and that dynamic is unaffected by AI capability.

name: Inbox by Gmail
one_line: Google's proactive email client with bundles, snooze, Nudges, Smart Reply and reminder-style task handling.
audience: Gmail power users and professionals wanting an assistant-like inbox.
stated_cause: Google shut Inbox down on 2019-04-02, saying it wanted 'to take a more focused approach that will help us bring the best email experience to everyone' after porting Inbox's best features (snooze, Nudges, Smart Reply) into the redesigned Gmail.
dissolved_by_2026: No. This was a platform owner consolidating two clients, not a technical limit. Inbox's proactivity features are now everywhere, which proves the capability was never the constraint.

name: Tempo AI
one_line: A smart calendar from SRI (Siri's birthplace) that pulled contact info, emails, documents and traffic into each event.
audience: iPhone-carrying business professionals preparing for meetings on the move.
stated_cause: Salesforce acquired Tempo in May 2015 and shut the app down on 2015-06-30, refunding paid users, folding the team into Salesforce's mobile and intelligence efforts.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Tempo's context-assembly job is trivial for a 2026 agent, but it died as an acqui-hire in a category where the value accrues to whoever already holds the calendar and CRM data.

name: Woven
one_line: A smart calendar with scheduling links, templates, travel-time and analytics on how you actually spent your week.
audience: Founders, executives and heavy-meeting knowledge workers; paid subscription.
stated_cause: Slack acqui-hired the Woven team (IP, customers and data explicitly excluded) and Woven shut down on 2021-05-28, deleting all production data. The founders told users their 'pace wasn't fast enough to achieve our mission with the current business'; paying users got prorated refunds.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Woven's own stated reason was growth pace against calendar incumbents, not what the software could do. 2026 agents make a Woven-class calendar better and also make it easier for Google and Microsoft to ship the same thing free.

name: Google Assistant Snapshot (and Google Now before it)
one_line: A proactive daily feed of cards - commutes, flights, reminders, packages, birthdays - predicting what you needed before you asked.
audience: All Android and Google app users; the canonical mass-market 'proactive assistant'.
stated_cause: Google quietly retired Snapshot with an in-app 'going away soon' notice and no replacement. Coverage was blunt: the feature 'was never given the attention it needed to thrive' - engagement never justified the maintenance of the prediction pipeline.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Google had the best data and the best models and still could not make an unprompted daily feed sticky. That is a demand finding about proactivity itself, and it is the single most important negative result on this list.

name: Pact (formerly GymPact)
one_line: A financial-stakes accountability app: get paid for hitting gym/diet goals, get charged when you missed them.
audience: Consumers trying to build exercise and food-logging habits via loss aversion.
stated_cause: Pact shut down in July 2017 owing users their earned payouts; the FTC then charged it with failing to pay - and in fact charging - consumers who kept their pacts, settling for a $1.5M judgment (mostly suspended for inability to pay) plus $948,788 in consumer redress.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Pact died because its payout pool mechanics did not balance and it ran out of money to honour obligations, then drew a regulator. That is a financial-product design and compliance failure; no model capability touches it.

name: Woebot
one_line: A CBT-based mental-health chatbot delivering scripted daily check-ins and cognitive exercises.
audience: Direct-to-consumer users seeking low-cost mental health support; 1.5M+ people used it.
stated_cause: Woebot Health retired the consumer app on 2025-06-30 and pivoted entirely to payer/provider/enterprise deployment. Founder Alison Darcy's framing: AI is moving faster than regulators - a rules-based, FDA-pathway product could not be shipped as fast as unregulated LLM competitors, and a consumer subscription could not be sustained against them.
dissolved_by_2026: No - it inverts. Better 2026 models made Woebot's careful, scripted safety architecture look slow and made unregulated competitors better. The regulatory asymmetry that killed it is sharper in 2026, not softer.

name: Amazon Halo
one_line: A screenless health band plus subscription that scored your sleep, activity, body composition and even tone of voice, with guided programs.
audience: Mainstream consumers wanting holistic wellness coaching rather than a sports watch.
stated_cause: Amazon wound Halo down, citing 'significant headwinds, including an increasingly crowded segment and an uncertain economic environment,' laid off the Halo team and refunded 12 months of purchases and unused subscriptions. Devices and app stopped working 2023-08-01.
dissolved_by_2026: No. Halo had Amazon's distribution and capital and still lost to Apple/Fitbit/Oura in a crowded category. Better coaching intelligence in 2026 does not resolve 'the segment is crowded and we are fourth'.

name: Arivale
one_line: 'Scientific wellness' - genome, blood and microbiome testing paired with a dedicated human health coach and personalized goal plans.
audience: Affluent health-optimizing consumers, initially at $3,500/yr, later $99/mo.
stated_cause: Arivale closed its consumer program on 2019-04-24, stating the shutdown was 'attributable to the simple fact that the cost of providing the service exceeds what our customers can pay for it.' Assay costs dominated, and fewer than half of customers stayed the year needed to reach profitability.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly, and only the coaching half. A 2026 agent replaces the human coach at near-zero cost, but the dominant cost was wet-lab assays - genomics, blood panels, microbiome - which no inference price cut touches. The sub-12-month retention problem is also untouched.

name: Google Duplex on the Web
one_line: An agent that drove real websites on your behalf - booking tickets, ordering food, checking into flights, even changing breached passwords.
audience: Android/Chrome consumers; the first mass-deployed 'agent that clicks for you'.
stated_cause: Google deprecated Duplex on the Web in December 2022 and retired its DuplexWeb-Google crawler, saying it was 'responding to the feedback we've heard from users and developers' and would 'fully focus on making AI advancements to the Duplex voice technology.' Reporting noted the approach required crawling and hand-tuning each site for hours daily and broke whenever a site changed or blocked the crawler.
dissolved_by_2026: Yes, on the technical cause. Duplex on the Web needed per-site scripted training; 2026 vision-and-tool agents generalize across unseen UIs without that. The remaining cause it does not dissolve: sites actively block automated agents, and that adversarial posture hardened after 2024.

name: Adept AI (ACT-1)
one_line: An 'Action Transformer' agent that took plain-English commands and operated your software - clicking, typing and filling forms for you.
audience: Knowledge workers and prosumers; demoed as a universal UI-driving assistant, never shipped broadly.
stated_cause: Amazon hired co-founder David Luan and most senior staff and licensed Adept's models and agent tech; roughly 20 of ~100 employees remained and the consumer/prosumer agent product was abandoned. Adept's own explanation: 'the astronomical cost of building and training their own models would have forced them to focus more on fundraising than on their actual product.'
dissolved_by_2026: Yes, for the stated cause. In 2026 you do not train a frontier model to build a UI agent - you build on one, so the capital wall Adept named is gone. What is not dissolved is that the incumbents who own the models now ship the agent themselves.

name: Rabbit r1 (the Large Action Model promise)
one_line: A $199 orange handheld promising a Large Action Model that would operate any app on your behalf by natural language.
audience: Consumers sold on an agent that replaces app-tapping; 100,000+ preorders at launch.
died: 2025 (LAM abandoned; device still sold, ~5,000 daily users reported)
stated_cause: The shipped device had four integrations (Uber, DoorDash, Spotify, Midjourney) against a keynote that promised universal app control; by 2025 Rabbit dropped the monolithic LAM story for 'Agent OS' plus a manual 'teach mode' where users record workflows for the device to replay. Reviewers could not name a task it did better than a phone.
dissolved_by_2026: Partly. 2026 agent models genuinely can drive arbitrary apps, dissolving the technical shortfall behind the LAM claim. It does not dissolve the product's other cause of death - a second device with no job the phone in your pocket does not already do better.

name: Android phone-automation assistants killed by the AccessibilityService policy
one_line: Third-party assistants and automation apps that read the screen and tapped buttons for you via Android's AccessibilityService API.
audience: Android power users wanting an agent that acts inside other apps on their phone.
stated_cause: Google gave developers under 30 days to stop using AccessibilityService for anything other than helping users with disabilities 'or risk having their apps removed from Google Play and their developer accounts terminated,' citing malware abuse of the API. Enforcement was paused after outcry, then repeatedly tightened; Android 17 blocks non-accessibility apps from the API outright, explicitly naming 'automation tools, assistants ... and launchers' as ineligible.
dissolved_by_2026: No - it got strictly worse. 2026 models can drive a phone UI perfectly well; the platform simply forbids it. The binding constraint is Google's and Apple's permission surface, and any on-device agent that is not the OS vendor's own still has no legal API to act through.
